The '''Ginn Jump''' was a part of the [[Arrowhead]] region, in [[The Slice/Legends|the Slice]] portion of the [[Core Worlds/Legends|Core Worlds]]. At some point between the collapse of the [[Infinite Empire/Legends|Infinite Empire]] around [[25,200 BBY]] and the [[Galactic Constitution Conference|foundation]] of the [[Galactic Republic/Legends|Galactic Republic]]<ref name="TEA" /> in [[25,053 BBY]],<ref name="TORE">''[[Star Wars: The Old Republic Encyclopedia]]''</ref> a [[Unidentified Duros hyperspatial physicist|Duros hyperspatial physicist]] romantically&mdash;yet relatively inaccurately&mdash;proclaimed the Ginn Jump and the [[Star system/Legends|star systems]] of [[Coruscant system/Legends|Coruscant]], [[Corellian system/Legends|Corellia]], and [[Alderaan system/Legends|Alderaan]]&mdash;which had long been inhabited by [[Human/Legends|Humans]]&mdash;as the four "vertices" of a region of [[Realspace/Legends|space]] that resembled a tetrahedron and was thus accordingly named the [[Tetrahedron]].<ref name="TEA" />

==Behind the scenes==
{{Quote|The four vertices of the Tetrahedron are Coruscant, Alderaan, Corellia, and the 'Ginn Jump,' which throws a bone to the fact that we're talking about three-dimensional space even though it's a pretty sloppy tetrahedron (acknowledged as such in the text).|Daniel Wallace|<ref name="Blog">{{Blogspot|subdomain=geekosity|url=2009/08/endnotes-for-star-wars-essential-atlas.html|name=Daniel Wallace's Geekosity|text=Endnotes for Star Wars: The Essential Atlas (part 1 of 5)}}</ref>}}
The Ginn Jump was first mentioned in the [[2009]] reference book ''[[The Essential Atlas]]'', authored by [[Daniel Wallace]] and [[Jason Fry]], which placed it in grid square L-10.<ref name="TEA" /> Wallace noted in his personal blog that the mention of the four vertices of the Tetrahedron region, which include the Ginn Jump, was meant as a reference to the fact that the ''[[Star Wars]]'' [[The galaxy/Legends|galaxy]] was, in fact, three-dimensional<ref name="Blog" /> despite ''The Essential Atlas'' generally only presenting two-dimensional maps of it for simplicity's sake.<ref name="Blog5">{{Blogspot|subdomain=geekosity|url=2009/08/endnotes-for-star-wars-essential-atlas_31.html|name=Daniel Wallace's Geekosity|text=Endnotes for Star Wars: The Essential Atlas (part 5 of 5)|quote=Another idea we dropped as too complicated was reflecting that up and down are also significant in determining systems, sector boundaries and the course of trade routes. We agreed that was a necessary simplification [&hellip;]}}</ref>
